angle: I was a BDR with 5 tools and a spreadsheet. Prioritizing my accounts took 10 hours a month
post_first_line: 10 hours a month went to prioritizing accounts.
linkedin_post:
10 hours a month went to prioritizing accounts.

Neema Zarrabian was a BDR with five tools and a spreadsheet, and the tools weren't the real problem.

The stack: an intent tool, a sequencing tool, a data tool, Sales Navigator, and a spreadsheet. Neema combed through all of them every single day.

The first 2 hours of the day went to finding data and writing emails. The last 2 hours went to building the call list for the next day.

Then came reprioritizing. It took 10 hours every month just to look through new accounts and rank them.

Neema was doing all of this from a parents' basement, switching between tabs and stitching together context by hand.

That manual grind is the reason Unify thinks about workflows the way it does. When everything lives in one canvas, you can build almost anything on top of it.

What's the most manual part of your day?

lesson.title: Count the hours your stack quietly costs
takeaways: Switching between five tools and a spreadsheet turns prioritization into hours of manual work.
Daily routines like data hunting, email writing, and call list building add up fast.
Reprioritizing accounts by hand can take 10 hours a month for a single rep.
lesson.exercise: Write down every tool you open to prioritize accounts, then time one full week of the data, list-building, and reprioritizing steps. Circle the one that repeats most and ask how it could run without you.

angle: It took 6-8 discovery calls to learn my target account was unintentionally breaking the law
post_first_line: It took 6 to 8 discovery calls to learn this.
linkedin_post:
It took 6 to 8 discovery calls to learn this.

Neema Zarrabian wanted one account more than any other, and the answer wasn't anywhere online.

Five years ago, Neema was working a named account list and kept coming back to one target in the Boston area, a large school district. The goal was simple: figure out why they needed us.

The answer only surfaced through discovery. Across 6 to 8 calls, Neema learned the district was unintentionally out of compliance because of its teacher-to-student ratio.

That detail wasn't in the news. It wasn't in any public research. It came from the chief of human resources, in conversation.

Neema's take today: a tool like Unify Chats could probably have surfaced that research and news much faster. But the lesson holds. The best insight on an account often comes from the person who lives the problem.

Research gets you into the room. Discovery gets you the real story.

What's the best insight discovery ever handed you?

Slide 2: Neema Zarrabian had a dream account in Boston
Slide 3: Public research gave no clear reason to reach out
Slide 4: Discovery revealed a compliance issue tied to teacher-to-student ratio
Slide 5: The source was the chief of human resources
Slide 6: Today, AI research can surface signals much faster
Slide 7: But the people closest to the problem still hold the best insight
Slide 8: Use research to get in, discovery to get the story

lesson.title: The best account insight lives with the person closest to the problem
takeaways: Persistence on a named account can uncover problems no public source reveals.
Discovery calls with the right owner, like HR leadership, surface insight research can miss.
Faster research tools help you start sharper, but conversations still confirm the real pain.
lesson.exercise: Pick one target account you've struggled to crack. List the role most likely to feel its core problem, then write three discovery questions to ask that person about what's hard right now.

angle: Outbound has two broken paths: 50 browser tabs or tens of hours building one workflow
post_first_line: Fifty browser tabs. That's outbound for reps.
linkedin_post:
Fifty browser tabs. That's outbound for reps.

There's a second path, and it's just as broken.

Here's the first one. AEs and SDRs work out of Salesforce reports and LinkedIn Sales Nav. A Chrome extension pulls contact info. Then they sift through every data point one by one, bouncing across those tabs.

The other path belongs to GTM engineers. They build very complicated workflows in a tool like Unify or Clay. You have to connect every data point, decide what happens in every column, and map out all of it before a single rep benefits.

So you get two options. Manual work that doesn't scale, or heavy building that takes a long time to set up.

Neither one is how outbound should work. One path burns rep time. The other burns engineering time.

I've watched teams bounce between the two, and the pattern is always the same. The work gets done either by hand or by hours of setup.

Which path is your team stuck on?
carousel: Slide 1: Outbound has two broken paths. Most teams pick one.
Slide 2: Path one: reps living in Salesforce reports and Sales Nav.
Slide 3: Chrome extensions pull contacts. Everything else is manual.
Slide 4: The result: 50 tabs open, sifting data point by point.
Slide 5: Path two: GTM engineers building complex workflows.
Slide 6: Every data point and every column needs a decision.
Slide 7: One path burns rep time. The other burns engineering time.
Slide 8: Which path is your team stuck on?

lesson.title: The two broken paths of outbound
takeaways: Manual prospecting means reps sifting through data points one by one across dozens of tabs.
Workflow-heavy setups in tools like Unify or Clay require deciding what happens with every data point and column.
Both paths cost time. They just charge it to different people.
lesson.exercise: Write down how your team does outbound today. Mark each step as manual rep work or workflow setup, then count how many tabs or columns it takes to get one account ready.

angle: Five minutes before a call: how an AE preps with recent news and growth signals instead of org-charting on LinkedIn
post_first_line: Five minutes before a call. No time to prep.
linkedin_post:
Five minutes before a call. No time to prep.

Neema Zarrabian's answer is not to org-chart the account on LinkedIn.

With a call with Vanta about to start, there was no time to map out verticals, find the CRO and VP of sales, or count BDRs. Instead, Neema asked for all the recent news relevant to the account, so the call could open with a point of view on where Unify can help.

The results were quick. Vanta is launching identity trust platforms, which lines up with how Unify thinks about the space. They just announced a Series D and crossed $300 million ARR.

That tells you they're growing and investing more in growth. It's exactly what you want to know before you join.

It also gives the exact timestamp and the sources, so Neema can read the article if needed.

The news also shows whether they're prioritizing enterprise or SMB.

Prep isn't about collecting more data. It's about walking in with a point of view.

What's your go-to prep step before a call?
carousel: Slide 1: Five minutes before a call. No time to prep.
Slide 2: Skip the LinkedIn org chart. It eats your prep time.
Slide 3: Ask for recent news relevant to the account instead.
Slide 4: Vanta example: a new identity trust platform launch.
Slide 5: Series D announced. Over $300 million ARR crossed.
Slide 6: Growth signals show where the company is investing.
Slide 7: Check sources and timestamps before you quote anything.
Slide 8: Enterprise or SMB focus? The news tells you.

lesson.title: Five-Minute Call Prep With Recent News
takeaways: Org-charting on LinkedIn is slow; recent news gets you to a point of view faster.
Funding and ARR milestones signal where a company is investing in growth.
Sources and timestamps let you verify the news before you bring it up on the call.
lesson.exercise: Before your next call, spend five minutes pulling recent news on the account. Write one sentence on what it means for them and where you can help, then open the call with it.

caption: Skip the org chart

angle: Which AI tool I use for CRM reporting and which for call analysis, and why I split them
post_first_line: Two AI tools. Two completely separate jobs.
linkedin_post:
Two AI tools. Two completely separate jobs.

Neema Zarrabian moved all Salesforce reporting out of Claude and into Unify, and the reason for the split is simple.

Win rates, conversion rates, and BDR team metrics now live in Unify. Neema used to run that reporting through Claude.

Claude still earns its spot for bulk querying the call recorder, like pulling what was said on each call.

Unify handles the TAM side: slicing and dicing it different ways, spotting accounts the team isn't reaching out to, queuing up good prospects for BDRs, and reviewing AE deals.

The pattern: one tool for what was said, another for what the pipeline data says.

Most teams try to force one AI tool to do everything. Splitting by job keeps each one doing what it's best at.

Which AI tool do you use for call analysis?
carousel: Slide 1: Two AI tools, two separate jobs. Here's the split.
Slide 2: Neema Zarrabian moved all Salesforce reporting into Unify.
Slide 3: Win rates, conversion rates, and BDR team metrics now live there.
Slide 4: Claude used to handle that reporting. Not anymore.
Slide 5: Claude now does bulk querying of the call recorder.
Slide 6: It answers what was said on each call.
Slide 7: Unify handles TAM slicing and accounts nobody is reaching.
Slide 8: It also queues prospects for BDRs and reviews AE deals.

lesson.title: Split your AI tools by job, not by hype
takeaways: Use one tool for CRM reporting like win rates, conversion rates, and BDR metrics.
Use another for bulk querying call recordings to find what was said on each call.
Use your pipeline tool to slice TAM, find unreached accounts, and queue prospects for BDRs.
lesson.exercise: List every AI task you run each week. Label each one 'call content' or 'pipeline data', then assign one tool to each group.

angle: 60-70% open rates, one meeting: why open rate is the wrong number to watch
linkedin_post:
60-70% open rates. One meeting booked.

That gap tells you everything about which number matters.

A question came up in a session: about 250 companies worked so far, one to three touches each, strong opens, and only one reply that turned into a meeting. Should the messaging change now, or do you wait for 7+ touches?

Internally, we focus a lot less on open rates as a performance metric. We focus on reply rates.

So the intuition was right: stop admiring opens and work on the reply rate.

Here's what we're doing about it. We're putting a lot of work into the copywriting skills our agent has access to, so the copy keeps getting better.

But the core principle is simple: make the message as specific as possible.

Opens tell you the subject line worked. Replies tell you the message did.

What metric are you watching that's misleading you?
carousel: Slide 1: 60-70% open rates. One meeting. Something's off.
Slide 2: Opens only prove the subject line got a click.
Slide 3: Replies prove the message actually landed.
Slide 4: We focus a lot less on open rates internally.
Slide 5: Reply rate is the number to bring up.
Slide 6: We keep improving the copywriting skills our agent uses.
Slide 7: The fix: make every message as specific as possible.
Slide 8: Stop celebrating opens. Start chasing replies.

lesson.title: Why open rate is the wrong number to watch
takeaways: High open rates with almost no replies means the copy isn't doing its job, even if the subject line is.
Focus on reply rate as the primary performance metric for outbound.
Make messaging as specific as possible, and keep improving the copy over time.
lesson.exercise: Pull your last outbound campaign and rank it by reply rate instead of open rate. Then rewrite the opening line of your message to be more specific to the recipient and test it against the current version.
